To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
binaural beats are represented by neuromagnetic gamma activity, which is strongest at low beat rates and at the beat frequency.
the human auditory system can process binaural beats up to a rate of at least 40 Hz.
binaural beats induce cortical responses in the gamma frequency range, and that these responses are largest at low frequencies and at 40 Hz.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the processing of binaural beats in humans.
the neural representation of auditory stimuli and how the human brain processes sound.
the neural basis of auditory perception, and we have used the binaural beat paradigm to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the perception of location, loudness, pitch, and roughness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the binaural beat response in humans is a complex phenomenon with a multitude of mechanisms and processes involved, including the opponent coding of sound localization, the modulation of neural firing by gamma oscillations, and the representation of sound location by phase-locked oscillations.
binaural hearing is a complex and dynamic process that can be studied in detail with the help of neuromagnetic recordings.

the binaural beat responses in the auditory cortex reflect the opponent coding for sound location, the gamma oscillations for precise temporal synchronization of cortical neural firing, and the bilateral phase differences for the separate sound representations in the left and the right auditory cortices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binaural beat responses are not only a function of the beat rate but also of the frequency of the carrier tones and the frequency of the beats.
we have identified a new type of cortical auditory response to the binaural beats that is not related to the percept but to the stimulus frequency.
the neural representations of binaural beats are not only determined by the stimulus rate but also by the temporal properties of neural oscillations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
binaural beats can be used to study the cortical representation of binaural processing and that the neural responses to binaural beat stimuli can be used to infer neural coding mechanisms.
the brain is capable of processing binaural stimuli in a way that is not limited to a single frequency range.
binaural beat responses can be recorded with magnetoencephalography and that the responses are largest in the gamma frequency range.
